strengths: Synth-SBDH addresses a meaningful clinical NLP resource gap with 8,767 synthetic examples, a 15-category schema, and annotations covering spans, presence, temporality, and rationales. The resource and demonstrated downstream benefits support a Findings recommendation.

The evaluation provides evidence beyond performance on synthetic data: models are tested on real MIMIC and VA datasets through classification and NER. Comparisons across several architectures, three-run means and standard deviations, and exact/relaxed NER metrics strengthen the empirical contribution. Improvements on rare classification labels are particularly promising.

Human review of all 1,755 synthetic test examples is substantial. Experts correct, remove, and add annotations and assess rationales. The category-level analysis and concrete failure examples provide useful information about omissions, unsupported inferences, and category confusion.

The appendices document the generation prompt, all 45 seed examples, GPT-4 version, similarity filter, label mappings, annotation guidelines, and substantial training configuration information. These details and the repository link provide a reasonable foundation for reusing the resource.
weaknesses: The comparisons establish benefits from the complete additional-training pipeline, but leave their source and cost-effectiveness unresolved. MLC receives 40 additional synthetic-training epochs before eight target-data epochs. There are no matched-compute controls, class weighting/oversampling baselines, or comparisons with simpler augmentation approaches. Consequently, claims about synthetic-data quality and compute-constrained effectiveness are stronger than the experimental isolation supports.

The headline improvements overstate the breadth of the gains. The 62.36% relative macro-F improvement is 35.03 absolute points for a weak prompt-based RoBERTa baseline. The striking housing result uses only 18 positive test examples; variability over training seeds does not capture uncertainty from this small test sample. For the strongest NER baseline, exact macro F rises only from 70.21 to 70.43, and standard ClinicalMamba classification does not improve. These results support useful augmentation more strongly than consistently large improvements.

The expert-reviewed benchmark has unresolved annotation limitations. The paper reports 77.80% human agreement without clearly explaining disagreement adjudication. Appendix D.1 accepts alternative categories when already predicted by GPT-4 but prescribes a more specific category when adding an annotation, making reference labels partly dependent on the initial prediction. Also, the 71.06% human–LLM figure includes added annotations in its denominator, whereas the LLM audit excludes omissions. These figures are not directly comparable, and the manuscript should consistently distinguish its silver reference set from a gold-standard benchmark.

The reasoning-distillation claim is weakly supported. DSS improves macro F by only 0.66 points for T5 and 0.58 for FLAN-T5, exclusively on the synthetic test distribution. There is no rationale-content control or real-clinical transfer evaluation establishing that reasoning was transferred. Real test rationales are unnecessary for evaluating extraction accuracy. Moreover, the downstream tasks do not directly evaluate the advertised temporal attributes or explicit presence-status prediction.

Exact reproduction remains limited by missing prompt-based classification templates/verbalizers, unspecified generation sampling settings, and ambiguous model-specific entries in Table 12. VA-SBDH is private, restricting independent replication of the NER findings. Dataset accounting also needs correction: the stated synthetic split sizes sum to 8,727 rather than 8,767.

Seed provenance and clinical inference rules need clarification. The paper claims to eliminate real EHR use, while Section 7.3 describes seeds as based on VHA notes and the generation prompt calls them collected from clinical notes. It should distinguish newly authored examples from adapted excerpts. Some seed rationales also infer absence of insecurity merely from employment or living with family; these assumptions can introduce systematic label bias.
